title: Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill (1985)
shortTitle: Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill (1985): opening excerpt
summary: A public employee who can be fired only for cause must get notice of the charges, an explanation of the evidence and a chance to respond before termination, followed by a full post-termination hearing.
notes:
Key line: The tenured public employee is entitled to oral or written notice of the charges against him, an explanation of the employer's evidence, and an opportunity to present his side of the story. (Justice White)

Citation: 470 U.S. 532 (1985).

sections.Parties: The petitioners were the Cleveland Board of Education, in No. 83-1362, and the Parma Board of Education, in No. 83-1363, both Ohio public school employers. The respondents were James Loudermill, a security guard dismissed by Cleveland, and Richard Donnelly, a school bus mechanic dismissed by Parma. Loudermill was also a cross-petitioner in No. 83-6392, challenging the delay in his post-termination appeal. Both men were classified civil servants under Ohio law who could be removed only for cause. James G. Wyman argued for the school boards; Robert M. Fertel argued for Loudermill and Donnelly.
sections.Material Facts: In 1979 the Cleveland Board of Education hired Loudermill as a security guard. On his application he stated he had never been convicted of a felony. Eleven months later a routine records check showed a 1968 grand larceny conviction. On November 3, 1980, the Board's Business Manager dismissed him by letter for dishonesty in filling out the application, without any opportunity to respond or challenge the dismissal. Ohio Revised Code section 124.34 made Loudermill a classified civil servant who could be terminated only for cause and who was entitled to administrative review before the Civil Service Commission. He appealed on November 12, 1980, and the Commission upheld the dismissal on July 20, 1981, about nine months later. Donnelly was fired by Parma in 1977 for failing an eye examination; the Commission ordered him reinstated but without backpay. Neither man was given a pretermination opportunity to respond.
sections.Procedural History: Loudermill sued the Cleveland Board and the Commission in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio under 42 U.S.C. section 1983, alleging that the Ohio statute was unconstitutional on its face for providing no pretermination opportunity to respond and as applied because of the delay. The court dismissed for failure to state a claim, reasoning that the statute creating the property right also specified the procedures, which had been followed. Donnelly's identical suit was dismissed as well. The Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit consolidated the appeals and reversed in part, holding that both men had been denied due process by the lack of a pretermination hearing, while affirming the rejection of Loudermill's delay claim, 721 F.2d 550 (1983). The Supreme Court granted certiorari, heard argument on December 3, 1984, and decided the cases on March 19, 1985, affirming and remanding. Justice White wrote for the Court.
sections.Issue: What pretermination process must be given to a public employee who under state law can be discharged only for cause? Does the state statute that creates the property interest in continued employment also define the procedures constitutionally required to take that interest away, as the Arnett v. Kennedy plurality had suggested? If some pretermination process is required, what must it include, and does the availability of a full post-termination hearing before the Civil Service Commission affect the answer? Finally, did the nine-month delay in Loudermill's administrative appeal itself deny due process?
sections.Holding: Respondents possessed property rights in continued employment under Ohio law, and the Due Process Clause, not the state statute, determines the procedures required to deprive them of that property; the bitter-with-the-sweet approach of the Arnett plurality is rejected. Some form of pretermination hearing is required. It need not be elaborate: the tenured employee is entitled to oral or written notice of the charges, an explanation of the employer's evidence, and an opportunity to present his side of the story, either in person or in writing, coupled with post-termination administrative procedures such as Ohio provides. Because respondents alleged they had no chance to respond, their complaints stated a claim. Loudermill's nine-month wait for a decision did not state a claim of unconstitutional delay. Affirmed and remanded.
sections.Reasoning: Justice White first confirmed that the Ohio statute created a property interest by limiting discharge to cause. He then confronted the argument, accepted by the District Court, that the legislature may condition the property right on the procedures it chooses to provide. Only three Justices had taken that view in Arnett, and later cases had confirmed that property cannot be defined by the procedures provided for its deprivation. The Court provided a clear holding: substantive rights are protected by constitutionally adequate procedures, and the categories of substance and procedure are distinct. Turning to what process is due, White applied the balance of Mathews v. Eldridge. The private interest in retaining employment is severe, since a discharged worker may lack the means to live and face difficulty finding new work. Some opportunity to respond before termination is valuable in avoiding mistakes, because dismissals often involve factual disputes, as Loudermill's own case showed. The governmental interest in immediate termination is modest, since an employer can suspend with pay when an employee is a risk. The pretermination hearing need not definitively resolve the case; it is an initial check against mistaken decisions, a determination of whether reasonable grounds exist. Notice, an explanation of the evidence and a chance to present the employee's side are enough given the full post-termination hearing. On delay, a nine-month adjudication is not unconstitutionally long per se, and Loudermill alleged nothing beyond its length.

topics.lrs-o-new-property: The opening identifies a for-cause employee and asks what pretermination process is due, supplying the setting without a completed answer.
topics.lrs-o-due-process-framework: The full opinion applies the Mathews v. Eldridge balance to fix the required pretermination procedure and rejects Arnett's 'bitter with the sweet' view of the property interest.

learning.separateOpinions: Eight to one on the principal holding. Justice Marshall concurred in part and in the judgment, arguing that where facts are disputed the employee should also be able to confront and cross-examine adverse witnesses before termination. Justice Brennan concurred in part and dissented in part, agreeing on pretermination process but urging a remand for factual development of Loudermill's delay claim. Justice Rehnquist dissented, reasoning that Ohio had conferred only a limited tenure defined by its own procedures and that no federal property right beyond that existed.
